lessons.title: Cash in Advance
lessons.body:
Cash in advance means the buyer pays before the seller ships. For an African exporter, this is the safest method: you get money upfront, no risk of non-payment. But many international buyers, especially in Europe or North America, will refuse. They don't want to tie up cash or trust a new supplier. So cash in advance is usually only for small orders, first-time transactions, or when the buyer desperately needs your product.

How do you get paid? Common tools: international wire transfer (SWIFT), mobile money like M-Pesa for regional trade, or online platforms like Payoneer or Wise. For example, a Kenyan coffee exporter might ask a German buyer for 100% advance on a $5,000 sample order. The buyer sends via SWIFT to the exporter's bank in Nairobi. Fees: $20-$50 per wire, plus currency conversion. Mobile money is cheaper for small amounts but limited to about $5,000 per transaction in many countries.

To protect yourself, always request payment in a hard currency like USD or EUR to avoid inflation risk. Use a bank that can confirm receipt quickly. Never ship until funds clearânot just show in your account. Once you have a track record, you can offer better terms like 50% advance, 50% on shipment. But for now, cash in advance builds your cash flow and eliminates risk. Just be prepared for buyers to negotiate. If they insist on credit, move to a letter of credit or documentary collection.

lessons.title: Open Account
lessons.body:
Open account means you ship first and get paid later, typically 30, 60, or 90 days after delivery. It's the most competitive terms you can offer, but also the riskiest. As an African exporter, you're essentially giving your buyer a free loan. If they don't pay, you have little recourse except legal action, which is expensive and slow across borders.

Why would you ever agree? Because buyers demand it. In many industriesâtextiles, agriculture, consumer goodsâopen account is standard. If you refuse, a competitor from Asia or Europe will offer it. For example, a Ghanaian cocoa exporter might sell to a Dutch trader on 60-day open account. The exporter ships 20 tons, worth $60,000, and waits two months. During that time, they still need to pay farmers, transport, and staff. Cash flow can kill you.

To manage risk, use trade credit insurance. Organizations like ATI (African Trade & Investment Development Insurance) or Euler Hermes cover up to 90% of losses if the buyer defaults. Cost: 0.3% to 1% of invoice value. Also, run credit checks on buyers through Dun & Bradstreet or local chambers of commerce. Start with small orders and short terms. Use factoring: sell your invoices to a bank at a discount (e.g., 2-5% per month) to get cash now. For intra-African trade, the AfCFTA might help, but enforcement is still weak. Open account works best with trusted, long-term buyers.

lessons.title: Documentary Collections: D/P and D/A
lessons.body:
Documentary collections are a middle ground between cash in advance and open account. Your bank sends shipping documents to the buyer's bank, which releases them only when the buyer pays (D/P) or accepts a time draft (D/A). D/P means Documents against Payment: the buyer must pay immediately to get the documents. D/A means Documents against Acceptance: the buyer signs a promise to pay in 30, 60, or 90 days.

For an African exporter, D/P is safer. Example: A Nigerian exporter sells $20,000 of sesame seeds to a Chinese buyer. The exporter ships, then gives documents (bill of lading, invoice, packing list) to their bank in Lagos. That bank sends them to the buyer's bank in Shanghai. The Chinese bank releases documents only after the buyer pays $20,000. Then the buyer can claim the goods. If the buyer refuses, the goods sit at the port, and the exporter must find a new buyer or pay return freight. D/A is riskier: the buyer gets goods before paying, so you're basically giving credit. But D/A can help you compete.

Costs: bank charges of $100-$300 per collection, plus courier fees. The main pitfall: banks don't guarantee payment. They only facilitate. If the buyer defaults, you must sue. Also, documents must be perfectâany discrepancy can delay release. Always use a reliable bank like Ecobank, Standard Bank, or Access Bank that has correspondent relationships. For intra-African trade, the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) is reducing costs, but documentary collections still rely on traditional banking.

lessons.title: Letters of Credit: Process and Pitfalls
lessons.body:
A letter of credit (LC) is a bank's promise to pay you, the exporter, as long as you present exactly the right documents. The buyer's bank issues the LC, and your bank advises it. This reduces risk for both sides: you know you'll get paid if you comply; the buyer knows they'll get goods if documents are correct.

Process: 1) Buyer and seller agree on LC terms in the sales contract. 2) Buyer's bank issues LC and sends to seller's bank. 3) Seller ships goods and prepares documents (bill of lading, commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, inspection certificate). 4) Seller presents documents to their bank. 5) Seller's bank checks documents and forwards to buyer's bank. 6) Buyer's bank pays seller's bank (at sight or after 30/60/90 days). 7) Buyer's bank releases documents to buyer, who claims goods.

Pitfalls: LC is all about documents, not goods. If there's a typoâsay, "sesame seeds" vs. "sesame seed"âthe bank can reject. You then fix and resubmit, paying fees. Common discrepancies: late shipment, missing signatures, inconsistent descriptions. Costs: 1-2% of LC value, plus amendment fees ($50-$100 each). For an African exporter, use LCs for large orders ($50,000+). Example: A Kenyan flower exporter sells to a UK supermarket on a 60-day LC. The exporter must ship exactly on time and present documents within 21 days. If not, the supermarket can refuse. Always ask for an irrevocable, confirmed LC from a reputable bank. Confirmation adds cost but protects against buyer's bank or country risk.

lessons.title: Bank Guarantees and Standby Letters of Credit
lessons.body:
Bank guarantees and standby letters of credit (SBLCs) are similar: they are promises by a bank to pay if you fail to meet a contractual obligation. They're used when a buyer or seller demands extra security. For African exporters, you might need a performance guarantee to win a big contract, or you might receive an SBLC from a buyer as payment security.

Example: A South African construction company bids for a road project in Zambia. The Zambian government requires a 10% performance guaranteeâsay, $500,000. The company's bank issues a guarantee: if the company fails to complete the road, the bank pays the government $500,000. The company pays a fee (1-3% per year) and may need to pledge collateral. Similarly, an SBLC can secure payment: a buyer in the US issues an SBLC to a Ghanaian cocoa exporter. If the buyer doesn't pay after 60 days, the exporter can claim against the SBLC.

Key differences: Bank guarantees are common in Africa and Europe; SBLCs are more common in the US. Both are on-demand: the beneficiary can claim without proving default, though this can be challenged in court. Pitfalls: If you're the exporter and you receive an SBLC, check that it's issued by a reputable bank and is irrevocable. If you're providing a guarantee, beware of unfair callingâthe buyer might claim even if you performed. Always use clear, specific terms: amount, expiry, conditions. For intra-African trade, the African Development Bank and Afreximbank support guarantee facilities. Costs: 1-5% annually. Don't confuse these with insurance; they are bank promises, not insurance policies.

lessons.title: Managing Foreign Exchange Risk
lessons.body:
Foreign exchange (FX) risk is the danger that currency fluctuations wipe out your profit. As an African exporter, you often get paid in USD or EUR but incur costs in local currency. If the local currency strengthens, your export earnings buy less. If it weakens, you gainâbut volatility makes planning hard.

Example: A Tanzanian coffee exporter sells 10 tons for $50,000, payable in 90 days. Today, the exchange rate is 2,300 TZS/USD, so you expect 115 million TZS. But in 90 days, the rate might be 2,200 TZS/USD, giving you only 110 million TZSâa 5 million loss. To manage this, use forward contracts. Your bank (e.g., CRDB, NMB) can lock in a rate today for a future date. If the rate moves against you, the bank covers the difference. Cost: a small premium or spread. For example, a 90-day forward might cost 1-2% of the amount.

Other tools: currency options give you the right (not obligation) to exchange at a set rate, but cost more (2-5%). Natural hedging: match your currency inflows and outflows. If you buy equipment in USD, your USD earnings offset that. For small exporters, mobile money platforms like M-Pesa now offer FX hedging in some corridors. Always invoice in a stable currency. Avoid currencies with high inflation, like the Nigerian naira or Zimbabwean dollar. For intra-African trade, the PAPSS system reduces FX exposure by settling in local currencies. But for now, forwards are your best bet. Talk to your bank earlyâdon't wait until payment is due.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: International Payment Methods for African Exporters and Importers

This practical reference consolidates the six core payment methods covered in this module into a single decision-support tool. It is written for African agribusiness managers, trade finance officers, and export desk staff who must choose, negotiate, and document payment terms under real commercial pressure. The guidance assumes you are dealing with cross-border transactions where counterparty trust, currency convertibility, and documentary compliance all carry material risk.

African trade finance operates in a distinctive environment. Intra-African trade is dominated by informal and semi-formal channels, while extra-African trade relies heavily on correspondent banking relationships that are increasingly subject to de-risking. According to the African Development Bank, the continent's trade finance gap is estimated at USD 81 billion, with SMEs and agribusinesses disproportionately affected. Choosing the right payment instrument is therefore not merely a commercial preference â it is a risk management decision that determines whether you get paid at all.

Payment Method Comparison: Cost, Speed, and Security

The table below compares the six payment methods across the dimensions that matter most to African agribusinesses: cost, settlement speed, security, and typical use case. Cost estimates are indicative and vary by bank, corridor, and transaction size.

Method Cost to Exporter (indicative) Settlement Speed Exporter Risk Importer Risk Typical African Use Case
Cash in Advance Low (wire fees only) 1â5 days None Very High First-time buyers, small consignments, high-risk corridors
Open Account Low 30â120 days Very High None Established intra-African trade, repeat buyers, supermarket supply chains
Documentary Collections (D/P) Moderate (0.1â0.5% of value) 5â15 days Moderate Moderate Commodity exports where documents control title
Documentary Collections (D/A) Moderate (0.1â0.5% of value) 30â90 days High Low Trusted buyers, seasonal agricultural commodities
Letter of Credit High (0.5â2% of value + fees) 10â30 days Low Low Large agribusiness contracts, new counterparties, high-value shipments
Bank Guarantee / SBLC ModerateâHigh (1â3% p.a.) On demand Low Low Performance bonds, advance payment guarantees, tender security

Sources: ICC Guide to Export/Import (2018); African Development Bank, Trade Finance in Africa Survey Report (2023); WTO Trade Finance and SMEs (2022). Cost ranges are indicative and vary by bank, country, and transaction size.

Foreign Exchange Risk Management: Tools and Considerations

African currencies are among the most volatile in the world. The Nigerian naira, Kenyan shilling, Ghanaian cedi, and South African rand have all experienced significant depreciation against hard currencies in recent years. For agribusiness exporters who invoice in USD or EUR but incur costs in local currency, FX risk can erode margins faster than any other single factor.

The table below summarises the main FX risk management tools available to African agribusinesses, their accessibility, and their typical cost.

Tool How It Works Accessibility in Africa Typical Cost Best For
Forward Contract Lock in exchange rate for future date Available via most commercial banks; limited in some markets Forward points; no upfront premium Known future receivable/payable
Currency Option Right (not obligation) to exchange at set rate Limited; mainly via international banks Premium (1â5% of notional) Uncertain cash flows, tenders
Natural Hedge Match currency of costs and revenues Widely accessible None Exporters with foreign-currency costs
Currency Diversification Invoice in multiple currencies Widely accessible Transaction costs Exporters with multiple markets
Local Currency Invoicing Invoice in buyer's currency Widely accessible None (but transfers FX risk to you) Buyers in strong-currency markets
Escalation Clause Price adjustment if FX moves beyond threshold Widely accessible None Long-term supply contracts

Sources: African Development Bank, Financial Sector Development Strategy (2023); IMF, Exchange Rate Arrangements and Restrictions (2024); WTO, Trade Finance and SMEs (2022).

â ï¸ CRITICAL SAFETY WARNING: Documentary Discrepancies and Fraud Risk

Under a Letter of Credit, banks pay against documents, not goods. A single discrepancy â a misspelled name, a missing signature, a date outside the permitted range â can cause the bank to refuse payment. In African trade corridors, document discrepancies are the leading cause of LC rejection, affecting an estimated 50â70% of first presentations according to ICC data. Always have your documents checked by a trade finance specialist before presentation. Never ship goods against an unconfirmed LC from a bank you have not verified. Never accept an LC issued by a bank in a jurisdiction with weak enforcement. Never release original documents to a buyer without ensuring payment or a bank guarantee is in place. If you are an importer, never pay against a copy of a bill of lading â insist on original documents or an electronic bill of lading through a trusted platform.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Assess counterparty risk first. Before choosing a payment method, verify the buyer's or seller's registration, trade references, and bank standing. Use the payment method as a risk mitigation tool, not a substitute for due diligence.
  2. Match the instrument to the relationship. Use Cash in Advance for new or high-risk counterparties; move to Documentary Collections or LC as trust builds; reserve Open Account for established, repeat relationships with strong credit history.
  3. Confirm the LC is confirmed and irrevocable. An unconfirmed LC from a bank in a weak jurisdiction offers little protection. Insist on confirmation from a prime bank or a confirmed LC from a bank with a correspondent relationship in your country.
  4. Check every document against LC terms before shipment. Create a document checklist from the LC and verify each item â names, dates, amounts, ports, descriptions â before presenting to the bank. One discrepancy can delay payment by weeks.
  5. Understand your FX exposure and hedge it. If you invoice in USD but pay costs in local currency, quantify your exposure and use forward contracts or natural hedges. Do not assume the exchange rate will move in your favour.
  6. Know your bank's correspondent network. African banks rely on correspondent relationships for USD and EUR clearing. Confirm your bank has a reliable correspondent and that your payment corridor is not subject to de-risking or sanctions screening delays.
  7. Document everything and keep records. Retain copies of all LC documents, collection instructions, bank guarantees, and correspondence for at least five years. In disputes, documentary evidence is your primary protection.
  8. Use bank guarantees for performance obligations. When you advance payment or require performance, insist on a bank guarantee or standby LC from a reputable bank. Do not rely on personal guarantees or unsecured promises in cross-border trade.

Further Reading

  • ICC Guide to Export/Import, 5th Edition (2018) â The definitive reference on international payment methods, documentary collections, and letters of credit.
  • African Development Bank, Trade Finance in Africa Survey Report (2023) â Data on the trade finance gap, instrument usage, and access barriers across African markets.
  • WTO, Trade Finance and SMEs (2022) â Practical guidance on trade finance instruments for small and medium-sized enterprises.
  • IMF Working Papers on Exchange Rate Arrangements and Restrictions (2024) â Analysis of currency convertibility, capital controls, and FX risk in developing economies.
  • ICC Academy â Trade Finance Courses â Free and paid online courses on documentary credits, guarantees, and trade finance operations.

This practical reference is intended for educational purposes and does not constitute legal or financial advice. Payment terms and regulatory requirements vary by country and transaction. Always consult your bank and legal advisor before finalising international trade contracts.

quiz.q: Which payment method is safest for an African exporter?
quiz.explanation: Cash in advance eliminates non-payment risk because the buyer pays before shipment.

quiz.q: What is a common tool for receiving cash in advance in Africa?
quiz.explanation: SWIFT wire transfers are widely used for international payments, including advance payments.

quiz.q: Why might a buyer refuse cash in advance?
options: B) They don't want to tie up cash or trust a new supplier
C) It is illegal in some countries
D) It requires a letter of credit
quiz.explanation: Buyers prefer to avoid paying before receiving goods, especially with new suppliers.

quiz.q: What is the typical payment term for open account?
quiz.explanation: Open account usually gives the buyer 30, 60, or 90 days to pay after receiving goods.

quiz.q: Which organization provides trade credit insurance in Africa?
quiz.explanation: ATI (African Trade & Investment Development Insurance) covers up to 90% of losses from buyer default.

quiz.q: What is factoring?
options: A) Selling invoices to a bank at a discount
C) Using a letter of credit
D) A type of bank guarantee
quiz.explanation: Factoring allows exporters to get cash immediately by selling invoices at a discount.

quiz.q: In documentary collections, what does D/P stand for?
quiz.explanation: D/P means the buyer must pay immediately to receive shipping documents.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of D/A?
options: A) Buyer gets goods before paying
D) It is illegal in Africa
quiz.explanation: With D/A, the buyer accepts a time draft and gets documents before payment, so you give credit.

quiz.q: Who guarantees payment in a documentary collection?
quiz.explanation: Banks only facilitate; they do not guarantee payment in documentary collections.

quiz.q: What is a common cost for documentary collections?
quiz.explanation: Bank charges for documentary collections typically range from $100 to $300.

quiz.q: What does a letter of credit (LC) do?
options: A) Guarantees payment if documents are correct
quiz.explanation: An LC is a bank's promise to pay the exporter upon presentation of compliant documents.

quiz.q: Which document is NOT typically required under an LC?
quiz.explanation: A buyer's passport is not a standard shipping document for an LC.

quiz.q: What is a common pitfall with LCs?
quiz.explanation: Even minor typos can cause banks to reject documents, delaying payment.

quiz.q: What does 'confirmed' mean in an LC?
options: A) A second bank guarantees payment
B) The buyer confirms the order
quiz.explanation: A confirmed LC adds a second bank's guarantee, reducing risk of buyer's bank or country.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of an LC?
quiz.explanation: Banks charge around 1-2% of the LC value, plus amendment fees.

quiz.q: What is a bank guarantee?
options: A) A promise to pay if you fail to meet an obligation
B) A loan from a bank
quiz.explanation: A bank guarantee ensures payment to a beneficiary if the applicant defaults on a contract.

quiz.q: Where are standby letters of credit (SBLCs) most common?
quiz.explanation: SBLCs are more common in the US, while bank guarantees are more common in Africa and Europe.

quiz.q: What is 'unfair calling'?
options: A) Beneficiary claims without valid reason
quiz.explanation: Unfair calling is when the beneficiary demands payment even though the applicant performed.

quiz.q: Which bank supports guarantee facilities in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Afreximbank and the African Development Bank support trade guarantee facilities.

quiz.q: What is the typical annual cost of a bank guarantee?
quiz.explanation: Bank guarantees typically cost 1-5% per year of the guaranteed amount.

quiz.q: What is foreign exchange risk?
quiz.explanation: FX risk is the potential loss from changes in exchange rates between contract and payment.

quiz.q: Which tool locks in an exchange rate for a future date?
quiz.explanation: A forward contract fixes the exchange rate today for a future transaction.

quiz.q: What is a natural hedge?
options: A) Matching currency inflows and outflows
quiz.explanation: Natural hedging means having expenses and revenues in the same currency to offset risk.

quiz.q: Which currency is considered stable for invoicing?
quiz.explanation: USD is a hard currency with low inflation, making it stable for international trade.

quiz.q: What does PAPSS stand for?
options: A) Pan-African Payment and Settlement System
quiz.explanation: PAPSS is a system to facilitate intra-African trade payments in local currencies.

quiz.q: What is the cost of a currency option?
quiz.explanation: Currency options typically cost 2-5% of the amount, as they give the right but not obligation.

quiz.q: Which mobile money platform offers FX hedging in some corridors?
quiz.explanation: M-Pesa has introduced FX hedging for small exporters in some African corridors.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a letter of credit over documentary collection?
quiz.explanation: An LC provides a bank's guarantee, while documentary collections do not.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a payment method discussed?
quiz.explanation: Barter is not covered; the module focuses on cash in advance, open account, documentary collections, LCs, guarantees, and FX risk.

quiz.q: What should an exporter do before shipping under cash in advance?
quiz.explanation: Always ensure payment has cleared in your bank account before shipping goods.
